Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan. Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards—the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, sixth and seventh editions (IMF 2009, 2025) and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014)— this loan is classified as a debt instrument based on the existence of a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, rather than on the expected source of repayment. Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability. Only where repayment is legally limited to those proceeds and the borrower has no obligation to cover any shortfall would the arrangement require different statistical treatment.
